skyline.text: Charles Booth’s study, before the disciplines went their own ways
How a non-specialist picks up the rhythm of papers
Heraclitus, and why two snapshots miss how change happens

brief.head: Increasing returns
brief.text: The more you know, the more new knowledge sticks, Ajay Shah said: “the learning process has increasing returns to scale”. So read, even if you forget. {075-C02}

brief.head: Stock and flow
brief.text: Amit Varma borrows two economics terms for creators. Flow is tweets, columns and episodes; stock is lasting work, like Milton Friedman’s *Free to Choose*. The best papers are both. {075-C04}

brief.head: Not every village
brief.text: Internal validity asks if your claims hold for the village you studied, Ajay Shah said; external validity asks if they hold elsewhere. Keep the two apart. {075-C14}

brief.head: Philosophers, Pvt Ltd
brief.text: Ajay Shah wants the word philosopher back for anyone eclectic. Plato and Aristotle studied everything, Amit Varma had said, and every label cuts a subject off. {075-C16}

brief.head: Uphill to breadth
brief.text: Formal knowledge production has overdone specialisation, Ajay Shah said, so almost everyone would gain from more breadth: “there is a nice lovely gradient to be climbed”. {075-C17}

thought.text: Our loyalty should be to questions.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, against economics’ lurches from one methodological fad to the next

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on a paper by Biju Rao
lead.head: Numbers, with the tears put back
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah set out to discuss two papers they both love. Time went by, lunch called, and they got through one. {075-J08}

The one they did discuss was Vijayendra Rao’s *Can Economics Become More Reflexive?* It argues that economics, anthropology and sociology, once part of the same quest to understand society, drifted into silos and stopped learning from one another.
Its central thought, Varma said, is the show’s own: everything is everything.
Rao, a World Bank economist known to his friends as Biju, has a line Varma loves: “The methods lead the questions, rather than the other way around.” {075-C05}
Once a field is loyal to one method, it can ask only the questions that method can answer. Incentives then lock the method in place.
## Four lessons from the field
Rao sets out four things economists can learn from ethnographers, and Varma took them in turn.
The first is cognitive empathy, Mario Small’s phrase: not imagining yourself in someone’s shoes, but “seeing another person as they see themselves”.
The second is to take words seriously. “Numbers don’t tell you the full story,” Varma said. “Words can tell you a lot.”
The third is process. Two snapshots of a place miss how change actually happens; the ethnographer stays on the ground and watches it unfold.
The fourth is participation. The very word “subjects”, Varma said, implies distance. Ethnographers make the people they study participants instead.

Rao learnt the first lesson in the field. In a village in 1992, women talking to his team blamed the state for their troubles for about a week, until trust was built and they spoke of beatings at home. {075-S04}
## Clubhouses and fads
Why did the disciplines split? Universities set up departments, Shah said, and promotion came to depend on publishing in each discipline’s own journals.

In economics, he said, one fad after another wins the journals and, through them, the appointments. There was a time for randomised control trials, for instrumental variables, for experimental economics. Scholars must conform or leave. Insisting on methodological purity, he said, is “very childish”.
## Close, but not too close

Shah was candid about his own leanings. He loves India, he said, and worries that rooting for it bends his judgement, so he takes refuge in data. He quoted a line he finds beautiful: “statistics are human beings with the tears washed away”. {#tears}
Varma’s answer was to go nearer: “you gotta get closer to that and see the tears, but not cry yourself.” {075-C13}

Shah, for his part, has always talked to people outside his formal research: practitioners in Bombay, officials, politicians, anyone with a factory to show. “Go out of your room and bloody talk to the people,” he said.

The episode had begun with a question about reading. Shah’s advice came from the economist Ed Glaeser: “read books for ideas, read papers for techniques.” Papers, he said, have chased rigour so hard that “the very pursuit for rigor has induced rigor mortis”.
Rao’s paper, Varma said, shows no sign of it.

second.label: How to read a book
second.head: Seeing like a reader
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the book he argued with on almost every page
body: One of the wildest reading experiences of Ajay Shah’s life was James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*. On almost every page, he said, he was arguing with the author. {075-S02}

Sometimes he disagreed. Sometimes he was unhappy, because Scott was going somewhere “completely antithetic” to what he then thought. Sometimes he offered other explanations. The book is not perfect, he said; it simply came when he was “primed and ready for it”. {075-R08}

He reads every paper the same way, as an argument with the author, rather than with the rote memory of Indian exams. Amit Varma’s verdict: Scott had cured him of “the fatal disease of seeing like an engineer”. {075-J02}

quote.text: I just remember literally page after page my mind would be bursting with the conversation.

photo.subject: James C. Scott
photo.hint: American political scientist, author of Seeing Like a State

second.caption: arguing with James C Scott

third.head: The title gives it away
body: When a paper studies Tamil Nadu but leaves Tamil Nadu out of its title, Ajay Shah said, be more sceptical of the work. “This is a guy grabbing for fame and glory.” {075-C18}
It is a disease of the advanced economies, he said, where papers on America do not put America in the title, though the work is about one narrow locale and the results do not generalise.
Shah said he does not share the arrogance of economists who believe they are creating universal truth. Every locale is different.
A modest title and a modest abstract, he said, speak well for the human qualities of an author. The others are “just like frat boys running for tenure”. {075-J07}
third.caption: grandiose titles

p2.title: Out of the silos
p2.deck: Vijayendra Rao’s paper on what economists can learn from ethnographers, read by Amit Varma and argued over with Ajay Shah

sections.label: The divergence
sections.head: The venue sets the tune
sections.caption: three disciplines drifting apart
body: Economics, anthropology and sociology were once part of the same quest, Amit Varma said: to understand society, and why human beings behave the way they do. Through the 20th century, driven by incentives, each retreated into its own lane: quantitative economics, cultural anthropology, qualitative sociology. {075-C05}

Vijayendra Rao’s paper opens with a work from before the split: Charles Booth’s study of the people of London, compiled in the late 19th century over, Varma thought, some 17 years. It used data, household surveys, interviews and observation, and covered employment, illness, family size and habits like thrift. {075-S03}

Then the methods began to lead the questions. Varma recalled the show’s episode on creativity, where the venue shaped the music: percussion in the open air, none in the echoing gothic churches of Europe. {075-R21}
## Scale or depth
The economist, Varma said, stays detached, works through survey agencies and gets scale. “You cannot do a weather report of, say, Karjat by only focusing on Karjat,” he said. {075-C06}

The ethnographer embeds in one community and gets nuance, but may miss the forest for the trees. The anthropologist Bhrigupati Singh, quoted by Rao, describes moving from hunter-gatherer to settled cultivator, “from impressions to expressions”.
~ Michael Burawoy, in *The Extended Case Method*, held that the positivist and the reflexive approaches are necessarily separate. Rao argues they need not be. {075-R04}

quote.text: If you look at the methods behind this, you couldn’t say that this is economics, or this is anthropology, or this is sociology.

sections.label: The first lesson
sections.head: Not your shoes, their eyes
sections.caption: cognitive empathy
body: The first thing economists can learn from ethnographers, in Vijayendra Rao’s account, is cognitive empathy, a phrase coined by Mario Small. {075-C08}

“Cognitive empathy is seeing another person as they see themselves,” Amit Varma said. If you see someone as poor and starving, your mirror neurons may kick in as you imagine their hunger. But how that person sees themselves could be radically different.
## A week to the truth

Rao learnt this in a village in 1992, where women spent a week blaming the state before trust let them speak of violence at home. Without that fieldwork, Rao wrote, they would never have thought of studying domestic violence. {075-S04}

The lesson, Varma said, is not to send a survey group, get some numbers and then “give gyan from a distance”. Talk to people, he said, stay with them for a while, and try to get a deeper insight into what is going on.
~ Varma noted the reflexivity too. When a husband dragged his wife from the room for talking to Rao, the researcher saw that his presence had changed the situation.

quote.text: But it is to actually understand from that person how do they see themselves.

sections.label: Lessons two to four
sections.head: Words, rivers and stones
sections.caption: words, process and participation
body: The second lesson is to take words seriously. Economists take numbers seriously, Amit Varma said, but the narratives people tell about themselves, followed over time, give a far better picture than numbers alone. {075-C09}

It must be done rigorously, not by drawing large conclusions from a few quotes. Varma expects machine learning to help sift through, say, ten thousand interviews from villages, where humans tend to see what they are predisposed to see. {#ml}
## Feeling the stones

The third lesson is process. Since the credibility revolution, Rao writes, empirical economics has been almost entirely focused on measuring outcomes. Two snapshots, Varma said, miss change as it happens. {075-C10}
No man steps in the same river twice, he said, recalling Heraclitus: the man has changed, and the river has changed. {075-J11}
Then, for Ajay Shah’s benefit, he quoted “your favourite Chinese personality”, Deng Xiaoping, on crossing the river by feeling the stones. {075-J12}

The fourth lesson is participation. In 2014, Rao and a World Bank team asked tribal communities in South Indian villages what mattered to them, and built their questionnaire from the answers. It shared only 17 per cent of its questions with the National Sample Survey.
~ That survey, Varma suggested, was possibly designed in Delhi by some bureaucrats.

quote.text: What is not done is often to do the most obvious thing, to keep a close eye on the ground
quote.who: Vijayendra Rao, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The incentives
sections.head: Fads at the clubhouse door
sections.caption: journals, fads and context
body: Once, Ajay Shah said, there were thinkers about the world called philosophers, and no disciplinary boundaries. Then universities set up departments, and hiring, firing and promotion created “tremendous incentive distortions in each field”. {#departments}
Senior professors told scholars to prove themselves in a few journals, each “the little clubhouse of that discipline”, and the vision narrowed. {#clubhouse}

In economics, Shah said, a fad wins, takes the journals and through them controls appointments. Every academic must then exit or conform. Diverse views often go unpublished, and the people who decide, he added, respond to incentives like everyone else.
## Not the intervention alone

Data has its own blind spot. Reading a paper that credited e-filing in one country with certain results, Shah objected that some 500 subtle details of law, public administration, invisible infrastructure, culture and norms were at work. {#fivehundred}
“It’s not the intervention that did it,” he said, “it is the intervention in all that context.” {075-C15}
~ His remedy is old-fashioned: panel data, observing the same firms and households across the country over and over, to make average claims about India.

quote.text: realistically we are all people and people respond to incentives and the people who control journals respond to incentives

sections.label: Learn the thumri
sections.head: Every paper is a thumri
sections.caption: how to read a paper
body: How should a reader spend their time? Entering a new subject, Ajay Shah said, first get the big picture through broad reading that integrates knowledge, and only then dive into narrow technical papers. {#bigpicture}
After dozens of episodes of *Everything is Everything*, he said, he and Amit Varma have a coherent view of field after field, so they are entitled to read one narrow paper at a time.
## Getting the rhythm

Shah’s first port of call for any search is Google Scholar, not Google. Even if you cannot follow a paper’s technical innards, he said, “in time you will get the rhythm, you will get the feel”. {075-R14}

The engine of a paper is IMRD: introduction, methodology, results, discussion. Read the abstract and introduction, get a sense of the methodology, skim the results and read the discussion. {075-C19} It is part of his recipe, he said, for reading papers in a very large number of disciplines.

~ The hosts closed with recommendations. Varma chose EH Gombrich’s *The Story of Art*, which, he said, is also the story of thinking and of stories; Shah chose Kenneth Clark’s *Civilisation*. {075-R11}

quote.text: It is a thumri and it is an art form, and you’ll get familiar with what is a thumri

side.boxText: Vijayendra Rao’s *Can Economics Become More Reflexive?* traces how economics, anthropology and sociology split apart, and offers economists four lessons from ethnography: cognitive empathy, words, process and participation. Amit Varma said it could be a book by itself. {075-R01}

contQuote.text: Our tears shouldn’t get into the picture, but we have to see their tears, understand why those tears are there, where they come from, what do they think about it.

stories.caption: the women who stopped lying
stories.kicker: Biju Rao’s fieldwork in 1992, as told by Amit Varma
stories.head: Trust first, then the truth
body: In 1992, the World Bank economist Vijayendra Rao, known as Biju, was with a group of researchers in a village, talking to women about their household income and their lives. {075-S04}
In a room full of women, a husband walked in, grabbed one of them by the hair and pulled her out. Her sin, Amit Varma said, was talking to Rao.
Rao realised that by putting himself in the situation, he was changing it. That, Varma said, is reflexivity.
For about a week, the women blamed the state. The schools were terrible, they said, and there was no good drinking water. {#week}

Then, once trust was built, one of them told Rao: “You have become our friends and we can’t lie to you anymore. Let me tell you the truth. We feel like we are in jail. Our husbands beat us all the time and no one helps when that happens.”

Tracked over time, the qualitative and quantitative data linked the violence to power within the family, to female sterilisation, which raised the risk of being accused of infidelity, to alcoholism and to dowry demands. The violence, Rao wrote, was often a rational choice to extract money from the wife’s family.

~ No economics journal would publish the mixed-methods version. It came out years later as two papers, one in a public health journal and one in an economics journal. “This is just completely pointless,” Varma said.
stories.why: Detached surveys would have missed the story entirely: without the fieldwork, Rao wrote, they would never have thought of studying domestic violence. And journal incentives split one rich study into two partial ones.

stories.start: Now, at the start of this great paper uh be two uh cites
stories.end: in a sense that that kind of work was part of a dying breed
stories.caption: Charles Booth’s London
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a study that belonged to every discipline
stories.head: The book no department can claim
body: In the late 19th century, Charles Booth set out to portray the people of London. The work took, Amit Varma thought, about 17 years, and filled a whole bunch of volumes. {075-S03}
It used data, household surveys, participant interviews and plain observation. {075-R03} And it was not done once: it was a continuous process over those years.
It covered employment, which is easy to ask about, but also circumstances that are harder to arrive at, such as illness, infirmity and family size, and habits: who drank, and how thrifty people were.
~ The result, Varma said, was a magisterial picture of London, its rich and its poor and how its neighbourhoods were evolving. For Vijayendra Rao, such work was part of a dying breed.
stories.why: Before the disciplines split, social inquiry used every method it could find. Twentieth-century incentives, in Rao’s account as Varma told it, pushed that kind of work aside, and the methods began to lead the questions. {075-C05}

stories.start: Okay, so for example, I constantly worry about myself that I'm so loyal
stories.end: I struggle with this and I run away, I take refuge in data
stories.caption: rooting for India
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the trouble with rooting for India
stories.head: If only it were Cambodia
body: Ajay Shah worries about himself. “I care so much about India that I feel it interferes with my objectivity,” he said. “Like, I’m rooting for us and that is a problem.” {075-S06}
If he studied Cambodia, he said, he would be a good scholar; studying India is dangerous. {#cambodia} Amit Varma assured him that he was still a good scholar.

The mind is a slippery thing, Shah said. Loyalty to traditional Indian culture, respect for one’s forefathers or simply wanting India to succeed can slide into propaganda and narrative battles that make him feel good. Cultural pride, he said, is damaging for objectivity.
~ And when he goes close to the experience of mass deprivation in India, the blood rushes to his head. “I run away,” he said. “I take refuge in data.”
stories.why: Honest scholarship treats one’s own attachments as biases to guard against, and choosing data can be self-knowledge rather than coldness. Varma’s reply was to see the tears, but not cry yourself. {075-C13}
stories.postscript: Later, Shah added that he and Susan know they cannot stay remote: “That’s one of the reasons why we hide in the data.” {#susan}

stories.start: I've never put it into any formal research methodology or research technique
stories.end: then you turn around and do the clean data work
stories.caption: a life of conversations
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the research he never writes up
stories.head: Four hours in a mall
body: Ajay Shah never brings people into his formal research. Papers, he said, are “formal set piece battles”. But he has designed his life around talking to the people in the economy. {075-S07}
One of the best places in India to study the Indian economy, he believes, is Bombay: it holds financial and non-financial firms, and everyday conversations with practitioners are rich with insights.

It takes many years of trust, he said, before people stop giving you their press releases. He talks to officials and politicians. Once, a firm’s head of marketing walked him through a mall for four hours, explaining the business. {#mall}

~ What people say about their reasons, though, is not necessarily the explanation. As Milton Friedman taught, Shah said, the billiards player never says he thought about Newton’s laws, yet behaves as if he did.
stories.why: Conversations on the ground bring common sense and hypotheses, Shah said; then you turn around and do the clean data work. What people tell you is the truth as they know it, which need not be the truth.

quiz.q: Which line from the economist Ed Glaeser did Ajay Shah offer on what to read?
quiz.a: “Read books for ideas, read papers for techniques”: big ideas now live in books.

quiz.q: What is cognitive empathy, in the phrase Vijayendra Rao borrows from Mario Small?
quiz.a: Seeing another person as they see themselves, not as you see them.

quiz.q: How much of the tribal communities’ 2014 questionnaire overlapped with the National Sample Survey?
quiz.a: Only 17 per cent of its questions were in common with the survey.

quiz.q: Why did Biju Rao’s research on domestic violence appear as two separate papers?
quiz.a: No economics journal would publish the mixed-methods version, so it was split in two.

quiz.q: What makes Ajay Shah sceptical of a paper that studies Tamil Nadu?
quiz.a: A title without Tamil Nadu in it: the author is grabbing for fame.

quiz.q: What art form did Shah compare a research paper to, and why?
quiz.a: A thumri: with exposure, you pick up its rhythm even without technical training.
